t: Count Substrings That Differ by One Character: Aligned-Pair Counting
o: Pick any non-empty substring of s and an equally long substring of t; the pair counts when their aligned characters differ in exactly one position. Occurrences count individually — with s = "aba" and t = "baba", the two a's of s pair with the three b's of t to give the six single-character pairs listed in Example 1. Example 2 (s = "ab", t = "bb") yields two single-character pairs ("a", "b") plus one length-2 pair ("ab", "bb") differing only at index 0, for a total of 3. Since both lengths cap at 100, even trying every start alignment and scanning forward with early exit costs about 100 * 100 * 100 = 10^6 comparisons — trivially fast. The refined O(|s| * |t|) solution anchors each valid pair at its LAST mismatched cell and counts with a suffix-run DP.
k: Every qualifying pair is anchored by its unique last mismatched cell, so counting mismatch-anchored alignments never double counts.
The mismatch count of an alignment only grows as it extends, so brute force can stop the moment a second mismatch appears.
DP cells split by whether current characters match: equal runs extend, while a fresh mismatch converts the preceding equal-run length into new one-difference pairs.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Alignment with Early Termination
a.i: Fix start indices i in s and j in t, then extend a window k = 0, 1, 2, ... tracking how many aligned characters differ. Every moment the running count equals exactly 1 contributes one valid pair, and once it reaches 2 the alignment can be abandoned forever because extending cannot remove mismatches. The triple loop stays around a million operations at these limits.
s: Extend k while both strings still have characters, counting mismatches.
Add one to the answer whenever the mismatch count is exactly 1; break as soon as it exceeds 1.
a.t: O(|s| * |t| * min(|s|, |t|)) — about 10^4 alignments scanned for up to 100 characters each.

a.n: Approach 2: Suffix DP Anchored on Mismatches
a.i: Anchor every counted pair at its last mismatched cell (i, j). Let eq[i][j] be the length of the equal-character run ending at that alignment and one[i][j] the number of equal-length pairs ending there with exactly one difference. When s[i] == t[j], runs extend (eq grows by one, one carries over from the diagonal); otherwise every perfectly matching prefix pair before the mismatch creates a new pair, so one gains eq[i-1][j-1] + 1, where +1 accounts for the bare mismatching character itself. Summing one over all cells gives the answer.
s: Allocate eq and one tables with one extra empty row and column.
Fill cell (i, j): equal characters grow eq and inherit one; unequal characters set one[i][j] = eq[i-1][j-1] + 1 and reset eq to 0.
Accumulate one[i][j] into the global answer.
a.t: O(|s| * |t|) — constant-time transition per cell pair.
a.sp: O(|s| * |t|) — two tables, reducible to O(min(|s|, |t|)) since only the previous diagonal row is read.

w: With these constraints brute force is genuinely acceptable; present the DP when asked to optimize or if sizes grew tenfold. Pitfalls: counting distinct substrings instead of occurrence pairs, treating zero-difference identical pairs as valid (exactly one means exactly one), and forgetting the +1 for the bare mismatched character. Natural follow-ups: generalize to exactly k differences (track mismatch counts up to k in the DP), or require the differing index parity constraints.
